Michigan property tax FAQ

When does the Michigan board of review meet?

The statute cited above says the second Monday in March, with alternative start dates a city or township may authorize.

How are Michigan property taxes calculated before you sell?

Michigan assesses property at 50 percent of its true cash value, and that half-value figure is the state equalized value (SEV). Tax is not charged on SEV directly. It is charged on taxable value, which for each parcel is the lesser of two numbers: last year's taxable value (less losses) multiplied by 1.05 or the inflation rate, whichever is smaller, plus additions, or the current SEV (MCL 211.27a).

This is the Proposal A cap, and it is why two neighboring houses of equal market value can carry very different bills. A long-time owner usually pays on a taxable value well below SEV. The cushion belongs to the owner's tenure, not to the parcel, and that single point shapes most Michigan sale-day tax surprises.

  • SEV is half of the assessor's estimate of true cash value.
  • Taxable value grows slowly while the same owner holds the parcel.
  • The millage rate set by each local taxing unit is applied to taxable value to produce the bill.

What happens to taxable value when the house sells?

A transfer of ownership resets taxable value. For the calendar year after the transfer, taxable value becomes the SEV, and the 5-percent-or-inflation cap then applies again from that new base (MCL 211.27a(3) and (4)). The statute defines transfer broadly: a deed, a land contract, certain trust changes, and a distribution under a will or by intestacy all count.

An heir who is the decedent's spouse, parent, child, sibling or grandchild can take a home without the reset, provided it stays residential (MCL 211.27a(6)(f)). A land contract is treated as a transfer when it is signed, and the later deed does not trigger a second reset.

The new owner files a State Tax Commission form with the local assessing office, listing the parties, the date, the real price paid and the parcel number or legal description, and the deadline is 45 days after the transfer (MCL 211.27a(10)). Deed recordings are also passed to the assessor at least monthly, so the reset does not wait on that paperwork.

When does the board of review meet, and how do you appeal in Michigan?

The first step is the local board of review. It meets the second Monday in March, and a city or township may choose the Tuesday or Wednesday after that as the starting date. Its opening session starts no earlier than 9 a.m. and no later than 3 p.m., lasts six hours or more, and the board sits 12 hours across that week, three of them in the evening. (MCL 211.30).

An owner or an agent can ask for a corrected assessed or taxable value, and the board must correct it if sufficient cause is shown. A nonresident can protest by letter, and a township or city may also allow resident protests by letter. The board mails its written decision, along with a notice about the tribunal, no later than the first Monday of June.

The Michigan Tax Tribunal hears the next level. For a house, the petition goes in by July 31 of the tax year, and the same date covers agricultural and timber-cutover land. Commercial, industrial and developmental real property, plus related personal property, has an earlier May 31 date. Other matters give 35 days from the final decision. A residential valuation case generally starts with a board of review protest. Disputes limited to arithmetic mistakes on a bill get 60 days from the treasurer's mailing (MCL 205.735a).

How does the principal residence exemption work when you sell?

The principal residence exemption (PRE) removes the local school operating tax from an owner's home. An owner claims it by filing a Principal Residence Exemption Affidavit, Form 2368, with the city or township assessor. Filing by June 1 lowers the summer levy, while a filing between June 2 and November 1 starts with the winter levy (Treasury PRE claim requirements).

The reverse step matters at sale. Once the home is no longer the owner's principal residence, Form 2602, a Request to Rescind, goes to the assessor inside a 90-day window. Filing late costs $5 a day, capped at $200, and the roll drops the exemption at year end of the filing year.

The same duty reaches other cases. After an owner dies, the personal representative or trustee files it. After a divorce, the departing spouse files it. After a lender forecloses, the former borrower files it once the home is vacated. Forms come from closing agents, assessors and the Treasury website.

What if the property taxes are not paid?

Township and city treasurers send the bills and collect first. A summer levy is a lien and falls due July 1, and interest runs on anything collected after September 14. Whatever is still unpaid on March 1 goes to the county as delinquent (MCL 211.44a).

A collecting unit may add an administration fee of up to 1 percent to a bill paid before mid-February. From February 15 until the delinquent return, the city or township may authorize that fee plus a 3 percent late charge (MCL 211.44).

The serious step comes a year later. Each March 1, parcels that were delinquent for a full prior 12 months forfeit to the county treasurer, and a $175 fee is added. A certificate is recorded at the deeds office inside 45 days. Redemption means paying everything owed plus extra interest of one-half percent a month, and it is open through the March 31 that follows the foreclosure judgment, or 21 days after judgment if the case is contested (MCL 211.78g). A seller with back taxes should request a written payoff figure from the county treasurer long before then.

EventRuleSource
Board of reviewSecond Monday in March, or the Tuesday or Wednesday afterMCL 211.30
Tribunal, residentialPetition by July 31 of the tax yearMCL 205.735a
Summer taxDue July 1; interest after September 14MCL 211.44a
ForfeitureMarch 1 after 12 months or more delinquentMCL 211.78g
Transfer noticeBuyer notifies assessor within 45 daysMCL 211.27a

What should a Michigan seller check before closing?

Start with the parcel's tax history and work outward. Closing agents ask for these same items, and a gap is cheaper to close early.

  • Confirm with the township or city treasurer which bills are paid, then check with the county office whether any year went delinquent.
  • Check the exemption status with the assessor, and send in the rescission form within 90 days of moving out.
  • Warn the buyer that the year after closing, taxable value moves up to SEV, so last year's bill understates what comes next.
  • To contest the assessment on a house, plan for the March board first and the July 31 tribunal date after it.
  • For an inherited house, find out whether the family exception holds the old taxable value before the heirs choose between keeping and selling.

Owners several years behind should act before forfeiture. After it, the parcel sits with the county treasurer, the foreclosing governmental unit takes possession only on the April 1 after judgment, and redemption ends at the March 31 cutoff.

More questions about Michigan Property Tax Guide

When does the Michigan board of review meet?

The week of the second Monday in March. Some cities and townships open one or two days later, on the Tuesday or Wednesday, and every board owes 12 hours of hearings that week, with three after 6 p.m.

When must a homeowner petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal?

Your petition must be filed by July 31 of the tax year. Residential cases generally begin with a board of review protest. Commercial and industrial real property follow an earlier May 31 date.

Do Michigan property taxes go up when a house is sold?

Often. A transfer of ownership sets taxable value equal to SEV for the next calendar year, wiping out the Proposal A gap the seller built up. The buyer reports the transfer to the assessor within 45 days.

How do I remove the principal residence exemption after selling?

Send Form 2602 to the local assessor within 90 days of ceasing to live there as your principal residence. Missing the window triggers $5 per day, with a $200 ceiling.

When does Michigan property go into forfeiture for unpaid taxes?

Each March 1, after taxes have gone unpaid for the prior 12 months or longer. The parcel is forfeited to the county treasurer for the amount owed, and redemption by full payment stays possible through the following March 31 after the foreclosure judgment.

What the official sources say

  • A principal residence is exempt from the tax levied by a local school district for school operating purposes if the owner files an affidavit. (MCL 211.7cc(1); source)
  • For taxes levied after 2011, the affidavit is due on or before June 1 for the summer levy or on or before November 1 for the winter levy. (MCL 211.7cc(2); source)
  • The exemption lasts until December 31 of the year the property is transferred or is no longer a principal residence. (MCL 211.7cc(4); source)
  • An owner must rescind the exemption within 90 days after the property stops being the owner's principal residence; late rescission penalty is $5 per day up to $200. (MCL 211.7cc(5); source)
  • An owner may retain the exemption up to 3 tax years on a former residence if it is not occupied, is for sale, not leased, and not used for business, by filing a conditional rescission form. (MCL 211.7cc(5); source)
  • Form 2368 Principal Residence Exemption Affidavit is filed with the city/township assessor; deadlines June 1 (summer levy) and November 1 (winter levy). (Treasury: PRE Claim Requirement; source)
  • A principal residence exemption exempts the home from local school operating millage, up to 18 mills. (Treasury: Principal Residence Exemption; source)

What the official sources say

  • State real estate transfer tax is $3.75 for each $500 or fraction of the total value of property transferred. (MCL 207.525(1); source)
  • County real estate transfer tax is 55 cents per $500 in counties under 2,000,000 population; up to 75 cents per $500 in counties of 2,000,000 or more. (MCL 207.504; source)
  • State transfer tax exempt: instruments with consideration under $100. (MCL 207.526(a); source)
  • State transfer tax exempt: conveyance from an individual to the individual's child, stepchild, adopted child, or grandchild. (MCL 207.526(j),(k); source)
  • State transfer tax exempt: instruments transferring property pursuant to or in lieu of mortgage foreclosure (not a subsequent transfer by the foreclosing entity). (MCL 207.526(v); source)
  • State transfer tax exempt: quitclaim deed to confirm title already vested/correct a flaw in title; judgments/orders of a court of record without specified monetary consideration. (MCL 207.526(l),(n); source)
  • County transfer tax exemptions include consideration under $100, leases, security instruments, court orders, boundary line instruments, and land contracts where legal title has not passed. (MCL 207.505; source)
  • State transfer tax is $3.75 per $500; county tax is $0.55 per $500 (up to $0.75 in counties of 2,000,000+). (MCL 207.525; MCL 207.504; source)
  • Register of deeds recording fee is $30 per document. (MCL 600.2567; source)

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Michigan land contracts have forfeiture and possession rules set by statute.

What the official sources say

  • Possession may be recovered by summary proceedings after forfeiture of a land contract only if the contract expressly provides for termination/forfeiture for nonpayment or other material breach; accelerated indebtedness does not count as money required to be paid. (MCL 600.5726; source)
  • A judgment for possession after forfeiture of a land contract merges and bars claims for money payments due at trial; a writ of restitution also bars claims for payments that would later become due. (MCL 600.5750; source)
  • State transfer tax exempt: land contract where legal title does not pass until total consideration is paid. (MCL 207.526(o); source)
Selling in Michigan?
We buy Michigan houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • Forfeiture notice periods under MCL 600.5728.

Michigan land contract FAQ

How is a land contract forfeited in Michigan?

See the statutes cited above and confirm the notice periods with an attorney.

What is a land contract in Michigan, and why does it matter when you sell?

A Michigan land contract is an installment sale: the buyer (the vendee) pays the seller (the vendor) over time and takes possession now, while the vendor keeps legal title until the contract is paid. Because title stays split from possession, a house under a land contract cannot be sold the way an ordinary owner-occupied home is, and every move depends on which side of the contract you are on.

The contract's own wording drives most outcomes. State law adds a few fixed rules about forfeiture, court timelines, taxes and recording, and those rules are the subject of this page. They come from the Revised Judicature Act, the Land Contracts act and the General Property Tax Act, all posted on the Michigan Legislature website.

  • A vendor who wants out can sell the right to future payments, pay off the buyer's side, or take the property back through forfeiture or foreclosure.
  • A vendee who wants out can assign the contract, pay it off with new financing and take a deed, or hand the property back.
  • A third-party buyer, including one paying cash, must find out who holds title and what is owed before offering anything.

How does a vendor forfeit a Michigan land contract?

A vendor can recover possession by summary proceedings only when the contract itself provides for termination or forfeiture after nonpayment or another material breach (MCL 600.5726). If the contract is silent on forfeiture, that route is closed. The same section says accelerated indebtedness does not count as money required to be paid, so a vendor cannot declare the whole balance due and then forfeit over it.

Before any court filing, the vendee must be served with a written notice of forfeiture (MCL 600.5728). The notice has to name the parties, give the contract date and the address or legal description, list the unpaid amounts with their due dates, and list any other material breaches. It must be dated and signed by the vendor, an attorney or an agent.

The vendee then has 15 days to pay what is owed and cure other breaches, unless the parties agreed in writing to a longer period. If the vendee does neither, the vendor may file for possession in court.

How long can a vendee stay after a court orders possession?

The wait depends on how much of the price has been paid. Under MCL 600.5744(4), a writ of restitution after a forfeiture judgment cannot issue until 90 days have passed if less than half the purchase price is paid, or six months if half or more is paid.

A vendee can still stop the process by paying the judgment amount plus taxed costs, and by curing any other material breach, within that window. Once a writ does issue, the same statute says the vendee's equitable right of redemption is cut off. That makes the writ date the real deadline for anyone trying to save the contract or sell their interest.

  • Under half paid: 90 days after the judgment before a writ can issue.
  • Half or more paid: six months after the judgment.
  • Payment of the judgment sum and costs, plus cure of other breaches, blocks the writ.

What happens to unpaid money after a forfeiture judgment?

Forfeiture is a trade: the vendor gets the property back and gives up the money claim. MCL 600.5750 says a judgment for possession after forfeiture merges and bars any claim for payments due or in arrears at the time of trial. If a writ of restitution issues, claims for payments that would have come due later are barred as well.

The vendor keeps a separate right to damages from the time of the notice of forfeiture. What happens to payments the vendee already made is a question for the contract and the court, because these sections do not set a refund rule.

Vendors who would rather collect the debt than recover the house can ask the circuit court to foreclose the land contract, since the circuit court has jurisdiction to foreclose mortgages and land contracts under MCL 600.3101. Any surplus from a sale under a foreclosure judgment goes to the court for the defendant or whoever is entitled to it (MCL 600.3135).

Can either side mortgage or borrow against a land contract interest?

Yes. The Land Contracts act lets a vendor or a vendee grant a land contract mortgage to secure any debt that a real estate mortgage could secure (MCL 565.357). It treats the vendor's right to payments and the vendee's right to a conveyance as real property interests. The same section keeps in force any contract clause that bars or defaults a mortgage, sale or assignment, so a due-on-sale style clause in the contract still counts.

A land contract mortgage is signed, acknowledged and recorded the same way as a real estate mortgage, and a recorded one is perfected without a separate commercial-code filing (MCL 565.358). For a seller this means a title search on a contract property may show liens against either party's interest, not just against the vendor's deed.

Which taxes and recording steps apply to a land contract sale?

For property tax, the General Property Tax Act treats a land contract as a transfer of ownership. Under MCL 211.27a(6)(b), taxable value is reset to the state equalized value for the year after the contract is signed, and it is not reset a second time when the deed is later recorded. The buyer has to notify the local assessor of the transfer within 45 days on the State Tax Commission form.

For the state transfer tax, MCL 207.526(o) exempts a land contract in which legal title does not pass until the full price is paid. The deed given at payoff is a separate document, so ask the register of deeds in the county what is due at that stage.

StepRuleSource
Notice of forfeitureWritten, signed, 15 days to cure unless longer agreedMCL 600.5728
Writ after judgment90 days if under 50% paid; 6 months if 50% or moreMCL 600.5744(4)
Money claimsMerged and barred by the possession judgmentMCL 600.5750
Assessor noticeBuyer notifies within 45 days of the transferMCL 211.27a(10)
State transfer taxExempt while title has not passedMCL 207.526(o)

How should you sell a house that is under a Michigan land contract?

Start by pulling the signed contract, the payment history and any recorded memorandum or mortgage from the register of deeds in the county where the house sits. Those papers tell you who can convey what, how much is still owed, and whether a default is already on the clock.

  • Vendors: confirm whether the vendee is current, whether the contract allows forfeiture, and whether a payoff or a negotiated assignment is faster than a court case.
  • Vendees: ask the vendor in writing for a payoff figure, and check the contract for limits on assigning your interest before you market the property.
  • Heirs of either party: the person's interest in the contract passes to devisees or heirs subject to estate administration, so the probate rules apply before anyone signs a deed.
  • Buyers: expect the closing to include a payoff to the vendor, release of any land contract mortgage, and a deed from whoever holds record title.

A forfeiture case narrows the time available. A vendee, or a buyer stepping into the vendee's position, who pays the judgment sum and costs and cures other breaches inside the 90-day or six-month window stops the writ and keeps the contract alive.

More questions about Michigan Land Contracts

How many days does a Michigan land contract buyer get to cure after a forfeiture notice?

Fifteen days, unless the parties agreed in writing to a longer period. The 15 days run from service of the written notice, and the notice must itself declare forfeiture effective at the end of that period.

Can a vendor forfeit a land contract if the contract never mentions forfeiture?

No. MCL 600.5726 allows summary proceedings only when the contract expressly provides for termination or forfeiture, or gives the vendor the right to declare one, after nonpayment or another material breach.

How long before a writ of restitution issues after a land contract judgment?

It depends on payments made. A writ cannot issue until 90 days after judgment if less than 50 percent of the price is paid, or six months after judgment if 50 percent or more is paid. Paying the judgment amount and costs and curing other breaches inside that time blocks the writ.

Does a land contract change the property tax on a Michigan house?

It can. A land contract counts as a transfer of ownership, so the taxable value is reset to the state equalized value for the following year. The buyer must notify the local assessor within 45 days of the transfer.

Can a land contract buyer sell the house before paying it off?

Often yes, but the contract controls. Check for clauses limiting assignment or sale, get a written payoff from the vendor, and make sure the vendor's title and any land contract mortgage are cleared at closing so the new buyer receives a deed.

Selling in Michigan?

What we could not confirm

  • Inflation adjustments to the small estate limit.

How does probate work when a Michigan homeowner dies?

Michigan handles estates under the Estates and Protected Individuals Code, known as EPIC. At death, a person's property passes to the people named in the will, or to heirs if there is no will, but it passes subject to creditors, family allowances and administration (MCL 700.3101). For a house, that usually means a probate court has to appoint someone with authority before a deed can be signed.

Probate runs through the probate court in the county where the person lived. The paperwork can be informal, handled through the court register, or formal, with a hearing. Informal is the lighter path and fits most estates with no dispute about the will or who should serve.

  • An informal application is sworn by an interested person and lists the decedent's details, the family members and the applicant's priority to serve.
  • A formal proceeding is required when anyone objects to who is appointed.
  • If a will exists, the original goes to the court with the application.

Who may serve as personal representative and sign for the house?

MCL 700.3203 sets a ranking. The person named in a probated will comes first, then a surviving spouse who is also a devisee, other devisees, the surviving spouse, and other heirs (MCL 700.3203). After 42 days a creditor's nominee can be considered, and after 63 days the state or county public administrator can step in if no interested person has applied, if no heirs are known, or if no heir is a United States resident entitled to a share.

Someone who ranks high can nominate another qualified person, or renounce in writing. Objections to an appointment can only be raised in a formal proceeding. Siblings who disagree about who should serve should expect a hearing, which adds time before any listing or sale.

An application for informal appointment is made by an interested person, and a creditor with a claim that cannot be enforced without administration may apply if nobody has filed within 28 days after death (MCL 700.3301).

Does the small estate affidavit work for a house in Michigan?

Usually not. The sworn-statement route in MCL 700.3983 requires the statement to say the estate does not include real property, and it covers tangible personal property, debts owed to the decedent and similar items, starting 28 days after death. It cannot move title to a house.

The court-order route is different. Under MCL 700.3982, a court may order property turned over to the surviving spouse, or to heirs if there is no spouse, when funeral and burial expenses are shown paid and the rest of the gross estate is $50,000 or less. Since 2024, a mortgage or other debt secured by real property in the estate is subtracted from its value, up to $250,000, when the court calculates that total.

The dollar figures are adjusted for inflation under MCL 700.1210. The Department of Treasury publishes the factor each year, so ask the probate court register or Treasury for the number that applies to the year of death. An heir who receives property by this order is responsible for the decedent's unpaid debts, up to the value received, for 63 days after the order.

What can a personal representative do about selling the property?

Once appointed, a personal representative may sell, mortgage or lease estate property for cash or on credit, including land in Michigan or elsewhere, unless the will or a court order says otherwise (MCL 700.3715). The same section lets the representative insure the property, make repairs and pay taxes and other costs of administration from the estate.

Within 28 days of appointment, the representative must notify heirs and devisees and the surviving spouse of the spouse's election rights (MCL 700.3705). Heirs who stay quiet about a sale can still be owed an inventory and an account later, so keep them informed before listing.

Special limits apply when the representative is the state or a county public administrator. The court must approve any sale of real property after a hearing, and fees tied to selling a property under tax or mortgage foreclosure are capped at 10 percent of net proceeds once those proceeds pass $30,000.

What if no one opens probate before the house is sold?

Michigan law does allow heirs and devisees to take an estate without administration. MCL 700.3901 says a successor can establish title by proving the decedent's ownership, the death and the successor's relationship. The catch is practical: a title company or buyer usually wants a court-issued authority, and the successor still takes subject to creditors' claims and family allowances.

Creditors have a defined window. If notice to creditors was published, claims arising before death are barred unless presented within four months of publication, and known creditors get one month after notice or the four months, whichever is later. If the notice rules were not followed, the window is three years after death (MCL 700.3803). A mortgage lender or lienholder is not affected by that bar, since the section leaves liens on estate property enforceable.

RouteWhat it coversSource
Sworn statementPersonal property only; estate must hold no real propertyMCL 700.3983
Small estate court orderGross estate of $50,000 or less after funeral costs, adjusted yearlyMCL 700.3982
Informal appointmentSworn application to the court registerMCL 700.3301
Sale by representativePower to sell land for cash or on creditMCL 700.3715

What steps should heirs take before listing an inherited Michigan house?

Work in order, because each step unlocks the next. A title company will ask for the court's letters of authority, and a buyer will ask who may sign.

  • Find the original will and the death certificate, and ask the county probate court which forms it wants for an informal filing.
  • Decide who will serve as personal representative, using the ranking above, and get any rival claimants to agree or renounce in writing.
  • Ask the county treasurer whether property taxes are behind, and ask the mortgage servicer for a payoff.
  • Keep the utilities on and the house insured while the estate is open, since the representative may insure and maintain the property.
  • Notify heirs and the surviving spouse within 28 days of appointment, then price and list the house.

An inherited house that passes to a child, parent, sibling or grandchild of the decedent may keep its capped taxable value for residential use. The property tax rules page explains how the uncapping rule treats family transfers.

More questions about Michigan Probate Process and Small Estate Affidavit for Selling Inherited Property

Can I sell an inherited house in Michigan without probate?

Rarely in practice. Heirs can establish title without administration under MCL 700.3901, but buyers and title companies usually require court-issued authority from a personal representative. The sworn-statement shortcut does not apply because it covers only estates with no real property.

What is the Michigan small estate limit for a house?

The statute states $50,000, adjusted for inflation under MCL 700.1210, and subtracts a mortgage on real property up to $250,000 when valuing the estate. The court-order route in MCL 700.3982 can reach a house, while the sworn statement in MCL 700.3983 cannot.

How soon must heirs be told after a personal representative is appointed?

Within 28 days. MCL 700.3705 requires notice to heirs and devisees, and to the surviving spouse about the right of election, no later than 28 days after the appointment unless a court rule sets another time.

How long do creditors have to make claims against a Michigan estate?

Four months after publication of the notice to creditors, or one month after notice to a known creditor if that is later. If the required notice was not given, claims are barred three years after death under MCL 700.3803. Liens on the property are not cut off.

Who decides who serves as personal representative?

The statute ranks the candidates: the person named in the will, then devisees, the surviving spouse, and other heirs. A court decides any dispute in a formal proceeding, and the public administrator can be appointed after 63 days if no one applies.
